Kosovo: Investigative Consulting

Investigative consulting for matters touching Kosovo means working with an accessible business register, a beneficial ownership regime introduced in 2024, a GDPR-aligned data protection law, and a business community where family networks, diaspora capital and cross-border links to Albania, Serbia and North Macedonia shape counterparty risk.

Overview

Kosovo at a Glance

Kosovo is a small, euro-using economy whose legal framework has been built largely since 1999 and is closely aligned with European Union models. For investigative purposes, that means comparatively good access to company information: the Kosovo Business Registration Agency (ARBK) publishes owners, authorised representatives and founding documents, and ownership data is available as open data. Personal data processing is governed by a 2019 law modelled on the GDPR and supervised by the Information and Privacy Agency. At the same time, institutions are still maturing, records may be held in Albanian or Serbian, and parts of the framework, including anti-money laundering legislation and the new beneficial ownership register, were still being implemented as of 2025 and 2026.

Organisations commission work involving Kosovo for several recurring reasons. Diaspora remittances and investment, particularly from Germany, Switzerland and the United States, fund real estate, construction and retail businesses whose ownership can be layered through relatives or foreign entities. Energy, mining, telecommunications and public infrastructure contracts attract international bidders who need to understand local partners and politically exposed persons. Kosovo is also a base for IT outsourcing and call centre operations serving Western European clients, which raises supplier and employee integrity questions. Because many businesses operate across Albania, North Macedonia, Montenegro and Serbia, matters frequently require parallel research in neighbouring registers and courts.

Jurisdictional Framework

The rules that govern lawful inquiry in Kosovo

Legal system

Kosovo has a civil law system based on its 2008 Constitution and codified statute, much of it drafted with EU and international assistance. Commercial disputes are handled within the regular court system, which comprises Basic Courts, a Court of Appeals and the Supreme Court, with the Constitutional Court ruling on constitutional questions. A specialised commercial court has been established in Pristina under recent judicial reforms. Arbitration is available, and international contracts commonly choose foreign seats. Court proceedings are conducted in Albanian or Serbian, so translation should be planned into any litigation support.

Data protection

Law No. 06/L-082 on Protection of Personal Data (2019) · Regulator: Information and Privacy Agency (AIP)

The law has been in force since 13 February 2019 and closely follows the GDPR, requiring a lawful basis such as legitimate interest or legal obligation for each processing activity. Criminal records, health and biometric data are sensitive categories processed only under listed exceptions. Controllers outside Kosovo that process data there through local equipment generally must designate a Kosovo representative. Transfers to jurisdictions on the agency's adequacy list, set by a decision of 17 April 2024 that includes EU and EEA states, the United Kingdom and the United States, need no authorisation if data subjects are informed; other transfers require an adequacy assessment.

Private investigators

We have not confirmed, from the sources reviewed for this page, whether Kosovo operates a dedicated licensing regime for private investigators or whether investigative work falls within private security legislation administered by the Ministry of Internal Affairs. TDSC therefore treats any field activity in Kosovo as requiring advance review by local counsel. Whatever the licensing position, the Law on Protection of Personal Data applies to surveillance, recording and the collection of information about individuals, and access to police, civil registry, tax and similar government records is restricted to authorised bodies. TDSC does not seek or claim such access.

Corporate & public records

The Kosovo Business Registration Agency (ARBK) maintains the business register. Public records show owners or shareholders and their interests, authorised representatives and their powers, and founding and change documents, and ownership data is published as open data. Financial statements are not held by ARBK; they are filed with the Kosovo Council for Financial Reporting depending on enterprise size. Law No. 08/L-265 on the Register of Beneficial Owners, published on 22 November 2024, requires a central beneficial ownership register at ARBK using a 25 percent threshold for companies, with public access limited to persons demonstrating a legitimate interest. Implementation timelines run from the law's entry into force.

Anti-corruption & AML

The Agency for Prevention of Corruption is the principal preventive anti-corruption body, alongside the State Prosecution and a Special Prosecution Office handling serious and organised crime and high-level corruption. The Financial Intelligence Unit receives suspicious transaction reports, and the Central Bank of Kosovo supervises financial institutions. Kosovo's anti-money laundering law was being replaced as of 2026, with a new Law on Prevention of Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism pending after a Constitutional Court decision; recent legislation also covers crypto assets and international targeted financial sanctions.

General information compiled 2026-11-04 from the sources listed below. It is not legal advice; TDSC works with qualified local counsel on questions of law.

Typical Matters

Where Investigative Work Involving Kosovo Concentrates

01

Diaspora-funded investment verification

Tracing the ownership and funding of real estate, construction and retail businesses financed by Kosovar diaspora capital from Germany, Switzerland and elsewhere, using ARBK ownership records, foreign registries and open sources to identify nominee arrangements and family-linked holdings.

02

Public tender partner screening

Background research on local partners, subcontractors and consortium members in energy, road, water and municipal infrastructure tenders, including politically exposed persons, prior procurement disputes and related-party links visible in Kosovo and neighbouring Western Balkan registers.

03

Outsourcing and supplier integrity

Due diligence on IT outsourcing firms, call centres and back-office providers in Pristina and Prizren serving Western European clients, covering ownership, litigation, reputational issues and the data protection posture relevant to personal data transferred to Kosovo.

04

Cross-border asset tracing

Supporting counsel in enforcement and fraud matters by identifying companies, shareholdings and documented property interests connected to a subject across Kosovo, Albania, North Macedonia, Montenegro and Serbia, working with local professionals for record retrieval and translation.

05

Beneficial ownership confirmation

Assessing who ultimately controls a Kosovo entity as the new register under Law 08/L-265 is implemented, combining ARBK legal ownership data, any accessible beneficial ownership extracts and corroborating sources, and documenting gaps where disclosure remains incomplete.

Engagement Standard

How TDSC Scopes Matters Touching Kosovo

TDSC handles matters touching Kosovo from Nashville through defined consulting engagements. Scoping starts with the question the client needs answered and a review of which Kosovo sources can lawfully address it: ARBK ownership and representative records, published court decisions, procurement notices and open media in Albanian, Serbian and English. Because many subjects hold interests across the Western Balkans, TDSC plans parallel research in neighbouring registers from the outset. Where documents must be obtained in person, court files reviewed or local enquiries made, TDSC coordinates qualified local professionals and works with the client's Kosovo counsel on legal questions. Personal data is handled under Law 06/L-082, collected only where needed, with transfers documented against the agency's adequacy rules.

TDSC has no office in Kosovo. Engagements are directed from Nashville, Tennessee; where work on the ground is needed, it is performed by appropriately licensed local professionals under a written scope. TDSC does not provide legal advice.

Questions

Kosovo: Frequently Asked Questions

What can the Kosovo business register tell us about a company?

ARBK records show a company's owners or shareholders and their interests, its authorised representatives and their powers, and founding and amendment documents, and ownership data is available as open data. It does not hold financial statements, which are filed separately with the Kosovo Council for Financial Reporting depending on company size.

Is the new beneficial ownership register publicly searchable?

Not fully. Law No. 08/L-265, published in November 2024, establishes a central register at ARBK, but public access is limited to persons who demonstrate a legitimate interest, and the register is being built on a timeline that runs from the law's entry into force. TDSC therefore corroborates control through other lawful sources.

Can personal data from Kosovo research be sent to the United States?

The Information and Privacy Agency's adequacy decision of 17 April 2024 lists the United States among destinations to which data may be transferred without authorisation, provided data subjects are informed. Other conditions of Law 06/L-082 still apply, and TDSC recommends counsel confirm the position where sensitive or employee data is involved.

Why do Kosovo matters often involve neighbouring countries?

Business and family networks in Kosovo frequently extend into Albania, North Macedonia, Montenegro and Serbia, and diaspora investors often hold assets through companies in Germany or Switzerland. Research confined to Kosovo can miss related entities, so TDSC scopes regional searches where the subject's profile suggests cross-border holdings.

Does TDSC need a local licence to work on Kosovo matters?

TDSC works from Nashville as a consultant and does not claim licensure in Kosovo. We have not confirmed whether a dedicated investigator licensing regime applies there, so any field activity is reviewed in advance with local counsel and, where required, carried out by appropriately qualified local professionals.
